A Minimal Supersymmetric E6\mathrm{E}_{6} Unified Theory

Abstract

We show explicitly that supersymmetric E6E_{6} Grand Unified Theory with a Higgs sector consisting of {27+27¯+351′+351′¯+78}\{27+\overline{27}+351^{\prime}+\overline{351^{\prime}}+78\} fields provides a realistic scenario for symmetry breaking and fermion mass generation. While gauge symmetry breaking can be achieved without the 7878 field, its presence is critical for a successful doublet-triplet mass splitting. The Yukawa sector of the model consists of only two symmetric matrices describing all of quark, lepton and neutrino masses and mixings. The fermion mass matrices are computed at low energy and a fit to the second and third generation masses and mixings is performed. We find a good numerical fit to the low-energy data. Thus, this model, having 1111 superpotential parameters, alongside the two symmetric Yukawa matrices, seems to be the best realistic candidate for a minimal renormalizable supersymmetric E6E_{6} unified theory.

1 Introduction

There are three types of unified groups (simple groups containing the Standard Model gauge group) that admit chiral representations for fermions: SU⁡(N)\mathrm{SU}(N) for N≥3N\geq 3 [1], SO⁡(4​N+2)\mathrm{SO}(4N+2) for N≥2N\geq 2 and E6\mathrm{E}_{6} [2]. The first two have been thoroughly studied in many versions, renormalizable as well as non-renormalizable, with and without supersymmetry. Strange enough, E6\mathrm{E}_{6}, the only exceptional group which contains chiral representations, has been mainly ignored over the last forty years. Apart from a few exceptions where symmetry breaking was analyzed (via renormalizable potential with 7878 and two 2727s in Ref. [3] and via renormalizable superpotential with 7878, 2727 and 27¯\overline{27} in Ref. [4]), only the Yukawa sectors have been touched upon without using explicit constraints arising from symmetry breaking [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10].

Recently, two of us have tried to fill this gap by suggesting a possible minimal renormalizable supersymmetric E6\mathrm{E}_{6} model [11]. The Higgs sector is composed of pairs of fundamental 27+27¯27+\overline{27} and the two-index symmetric 351′+351′¯351^{\prime}+\overline{351^{\prime}} representations. Much to our surprise we found that, although successful in the symmetry breaking pattern to the Standard Model (SM) gauge group, this sector is unable to provide two light Higgs doublets of the minimal supersymmetric Standard Model (MSSM), or technically said, to perform the doublet-triplet (DT) splitting. The impossibility of DT splitting was due to the identical nature of the expressions for a massless doublet and for a massless triplet; this result was obtained by an explicit computation, and we are not aware of a shortcut explanation of this unusual feature.44 4 The sparsity of SU(5) breaking vacuum expectation values in the respective mass matrices is likely to be the fundamental origin of this problem. To put this result in perspective, consider the minimal renormalizable supersymmetric breaking sectors (able to break to the SM group) for other groups. In the minimal renormalizable SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5) superpotential (consisting of the adjoint 2424), there are no SM doublets. In the corresponding minimal SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10) case (made out of 210210, 126126 and 126¯\overline{126}) one has in principle enough doublets, but only one (in 126¯\overline{126}) is coupled to fermions. In a minimal E6\mathrm{E}_{6} case with 27+27¯+351′+351′¯27+\overline{27}+351^{\prime}+\overline{351^{\prime}}, there are many more doublets which couple to fermions, yet the naive DT splitting fails (a completely different approach to DT splitting in E6\mathrm{E}_{6} can be found in [12]). We thus proposed in [11] to add another 27+27¯27+\overline{27} pair. In this way, the Yukawa sector consisted of three Yukawa matrices: the matter fields (3 copies of 27F27_{F}) have one coupling to the 351′¯\overline{351^{\prime}} and a coupling to each of the two Higgs-like 2727s. Though we did not perform it explicitly, we strongly believe that in this model a realistic fit of the Yukawa sector is possible to obtain, but the model is essentially not predictive due to the large number of free parameters in the three Yukawa matrices.

The purpose of this paper is to find an E6\mathrm{E}_{6} theory with only two Yukawa matrices and thus a simpler Yukawa sector than the model in [11], while keeping the symmetry breaking sector as simple as possible. The idea is to add to the minimal breaking sector (instead of the extra 27+27¯27+\overline{27} pair) another multiplet, which preferably has the following properties:

  1. 1.

    It does not couple to the matter bilinears (and so is not a 2727, 351¯\overline{351} or 351′¯\overline{351^{\prime}}).

  2. 2.

    It contributes to the symmetry breaking vacuum.

  3. 3.

    It increases the size of the mass matrices for weak doublets and/or color triplets.

The minimal such multiplet is the adjoint representation 7878, for which all of the above properties hold true. We will see that its inclusion is enough to allow the doublet-triplet splitting in the theory, thus leading to a theory with the correct (SM) vacuum and the correct (MSSM) low energy field theory.

The Yukawa sector in this model consists of two matrices only. Assuming 3 generations, the down quark and charged lepton sectors have 3 extra vector-like fields, while the neutrino sector has 3 extra vector-like lepton doublet-antidoublet pairs, as well as 6 SM singlets, all coming from the extra fields in the decomposition of the fundamental 27 into the SM subgroup. The projection of all these fields into the usual 3 light generations will be performed explicitly and shown, in the simplified case of only two generations, to provide a realistic fit of the masses and mixing angles.

Special attention needs to be paid to the overall neutrino mass scale. In minimal SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10) [13, 14, 15] this scale poses a serious problem and eventually rules out the low-energy supersymmetry scenario [16, 17, 18, 19]: a too low SU​(2)R\mathrm{SU}(2)_{R} breaking is disallowed by unification constraints and/or D=6D=6 proton decay [20], while a too large breaking scale makes the right-handed neutrinos too heavy and thus the seesaw mechanism ineffective to produce a large enough scale for the light neutrinos. In our model this conclusion is avoidable because there are many possible fields that can break SU​(2)R\mathrm{SU}(2)_{R}. While the neutrino mass scale can be adjusted by choosing the vacuum expectation value (VEV) of the (1,3,10)(1,3,10) of the Pati-Salam (PS) SU​(2)L×SU​(2)R×SU​(4)C\mathrm{SU}(2)_{L}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{R}\times\mathrm{SU}(4)_{C}, located in the 126¯\overline{126} of SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10), which in turn is found in the 351′¯\overline{351^{\prime}} of E6\mathrm{E}_{6}, all other fields’ masses depend also on several other VEVs. We can thus arrange a lighter VEV of this (1,3,10)(1,3,10) still avoiding dramatic changes in the renormalization group (RG) gauge running.

We arrange the paper in the following way: we define the model and specify the terms in the superpotential in section 2. We find a suitable vacuum solution, which breaks E6\mathrm{E}_{6} into the SM group in section 3, perform the doublet-triplet splitting in section 4 and compute the mass matrices in the Yukawa sector and identify the low energy content of the theory in section 5. We then use the obtained results to perform a 22 generation fit of the masses and mixing angles in section 6. We finish with a discussion in section 7. Five different appendices collect various definitions and technical results. All explicit computation in E6\mathrm{E}_{6} has been performed using methods from [21] and [11]; also, [22, 23, 24] might also prove useful to the reader.

For ease of use we stick to the following color convention in this paper: red denotes VEVs coming from the spontaneous symmetry breaking of the unified theory at the scale MG​U​TM_{GUT}, while blue denotes VEVs coming from electroweak (EW) symmetry breaking at the scale mE​Wm_{EW}.

2 Defining the model

The renormalizable E6E_{6} SUSY GUT that we consider here is an alternative to the model in [11]. It is motivated by the fact that the minimal Higgs sector in a renormalizable SUSY E6\mathrm{E}_{6} model, which can break E6\mathrm{E}_{6} to the Standard Model, is 351′+351′¯+27+27¯351^{\prime}+\overline{351^{\prime}}+27+\overline{27}. This minimal breaking sector cannot accommodate doublet-triplet splitting, however, and therefore needs to be extended to get a realistic model. One possible extension is an addition of a 27+27¯27+\overline{27} pair, which was analyzed in [11], while an alternative, taken in this paper, is to extend it by the representation 7878 instead. The Yukawa sector in the present model will consist of only two matrices, unlike that in [11], which has three matrices.

Our renormalizable E6\mathrm{E}_{6} model thus contains the following:

  • •

    The “fermionic sector” of three copies of a chiral supermultiplet 2727, denoted by 27Fi27_{F}^{i}, with i=1,2,3i=1,2,3. Also, we assume a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} matter parity, under which the 27F27_{F} are −1-1, and the remaining chiral superfields are +1+1. With this symmetry, the ansatz ⟨27F⟩=0\langle 27_{F}\rangle=0 is consistent with the equations of motion, which we shall adopt.

  • •

    The “breaking sector” consisting of 351′+351′¯+27+27¯+78351^{\prime}+\overline{351^{\prime}}+27+\overline{27}+78.

The model under consideration is supersymmetric. The problem of SUSY breaking will not be considered, since it is (usually) an orthogonal problem to breaking the gauge group. One can imagine however, that whatever the detailed mechanism of SUSY breaking might be, we get soft SUSY breaking terms at energies not far above mEWm_{\textrm{EW}}, such that we get automatic unification of gauge couplings at MGUTM_{\textrm{GUT}} assuming no extra particle states up to the unification scale. The effective low energy theory of our model will thus be MSSM. The soft SUSY breaking terms do not give contributions to the fermion masses at tree level. A fit to fermion masses and mixings can then be done without specifying the details of SUSY breaking, although the RG evolution of these parameters does depend on the SUSY scale (which we assume is of order few TeV).

The full superpotential of our model is

Wfull\displaystyle W_{\textrm{full}} =m27​ 27​27¯+m351′​ 351′​351′¯+m78​ 78 78\displaystyle=m_{27}\;27\;\overline{27}\;+\;m_{351^{\prime}}\;351^{\prime}\;\overline{351^{\prime}}\;+\;m_{78}\;78\;78
+λ1​ 351′3+λ2​351′¯3+λ3​ 272​351′¯+λ4​27¯2​ 351′\displaystyle\quad+\;\lambda_{1}\;351^{\prime 3}\;+\;\lambda_{2}\;\overline{351^{\prime}}^{3}\;+\;\lambda_{3}\;27^{2}\;\overline{351^{\prime}}\;+\;\lambda_{4}\;\overline{27}^{2}\;351^{\prime}

Note that the definitions of 351′351^{\prime} and 351′¯\overline{351^{\prime}} used here are switched compared to Slansky’s defintions [25].

3 Spontaneous symmetry breaking

3.1 Equations of motion

The Higgs sector 351′+351′¯+27+27¯+78351^{\prime}+\overline{351^{\prime}}+27+\overline{27}+78 forms a realistic Higgs sector, which is able to break the gauge group from E6E_{6} to SU​(3)C×SU​(2)L×U​(1)Y\mathrm{SU}(3)_{C}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{L}\times\mathrm{U}(1)_{Y}. We provide just such a vacuum below.

First, note the decompositions of 2727, 7878 and 351′351^{\prime} under SO⁡(10)×U⁡(1)\mathrm{SO}(10)\times\mathrm{U}(1):

27\displaystyle 27 =16​(1)+10​(−2)+1​(4),\displaystyle=16(1)+10(-2)+1(4), (2)
78\displaystyle 78 =45​(0)+16​(−3)+16¯​(3)+1​(0),\displaystyle=45(0)+16(-3)+\overline{16}(3)+1(0), (3)
351′\displaystyle 351^{\prime} =1​(8)+10​(2)+16​(5)+54​(−4)+126​(2)+144¯​(−1).\displaystyle=1(8)+10(2)+16(5)+54(-4)+126(2)+\overline{144}(-1). (4)

The representation 351′351^{\prime} contains 55 SM singlets, 33 of which are SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5) singlets (in 11, 1616 and 126126 of SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10)), and 22 are part of a 2424 under SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5) (in 5454 and 144¯\overline{144} of SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10)). Similarly, the representation 7878 also has 55 singlets, with one being a 2424 under SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5) (the one in 4545 of SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10)), while the remaining ones are singlets under SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5) (the 11, 1616 and 16¯\overline{16} of SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10), as well as another one in the 4545). The Higgs sector 351′+351′¯+27+27¯+78351^{\prime}+\overline{351^{\prime}}+27+\overline{27}+78 therefore contains 5+5+2+2+5=195+5+2+2+5=19 singlets in total. We list their VEVs55 5 Notice that the Standard Model singlet VEVs have been denoted by u1u_{1}, u2u_{2}, vv, ww and yy. 3.2 A specific vacuum solution

In this section, we obtain a vacuum solution which breaks the gauge group to the Standard Model group SU​(3)C×SU​(2)L×U​(1)Y\mathrm{SU}(3)_{C}\times\mathrm{SU}(2)_{L}\times\mathrm{U}(1)_{Y}. Due to the complexity of the equations we are unable to provide a full classification of vacua; a short discussion on alternative vacua can be found in Appendix D.

The equations of motion in SUSY models are

Da\displaystyle D^{a} =0,\displaystyle=0, (26)
Fϕ\displaystyle F_{\phi} =0,\displaystyle=0, (27)

with the usual definition of the FF-term:

Fϕ:=∂W∂ϕ.\displaystyle F_{\phi}:=\frac{\partial W}{\partial\phi}. (28)

In our case, there are 1919 Standard Model singlets in the Higgs sector, giving 1919 non-trivial FF-terms, which can be easily reconstructed from the superpotential in equation (5) and the all-singlet terms of the invariants given by equations (6)–(16). The non-trivial DD-terms are given by equations (23)–(25).

To obtain a vacuum solution, we perform the following steps:

    Note that vv and ww are determined, once AA is fixed. We can therefore see that f4∝1/e4f_{4}\propto 1/e_{4}, e3∝f42∝1/e42e_{3}\propto f_{4}^{2}\propto 1/e_{4}^{2} and f3∝e42f_{3}\propto e_{4}^{2}. Similarly, d2∝1/c2d_{2}\propto 1/c_{2}, e1∝c2/d2∝c22e_{1}\propto c_{2}/d_{2}\propto c_{2}^{2} and f1∝d2/c2∝1/c22f_{1}\propto d_{2}/c_{2}\propto 1/c_{2}^{2}, DI​ID^{II} is a quartic polynomial in c2c_{2} independent of e4e_{4}; the constant coefficient will be negative (the f1f_{1} term), while the highest order coefficient in |c2|2|c_{2}|^{2} is positive (the e1e_{1} term), which again guarantees a real solution c2>0c_{2}>0.

The solution above does indeed break E6\mathrm{E}_{6} into the Standard Model group. This can be checked by explicitly computing the gauge boson masses, found in Table 8 of Appendix A. It is possible to further illuminate this result by considering that under the standard embeddings of the E6\mathrm{E}_{6} subgroups from Table 1, the SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5) breaking in our solution is solely due to non-vanishing VEVs e4e_{4} and f4f_{4}.

4 Doublet-triplet splitting

We tackle now the issue of doublet-triplet splitting. We denote the doublets and antidoublets by D∼(1,2,+1/2)D\sim(1,2,+1/2) and D¯∼(1,2,−1/2)\overline{D}\sim(1,2,-1/2), while the triplets and antitriplets are denoted by T∼(3,1,−1/3)T\sim(3,1,-1/3) and T¯∼(3¯,1,+1/3)\overline{T}\sim(\bar{3},1,+1/3). The detailed labels of these states are given in Table 10 of Appendix B.

In the Higgs sector of our model, there are 1212 doublet-antidoublet pairs and 1313 triplet-antitriplet pairs. This is one extra pair of each compared to the renormalizable model with the Higgs sector 351′+351′¯+27+27¯351^{\prime}+\overline{351^{\prime}}+27+\overline{27}, in which doublet-triplet splitting surprisingly fails (see [11] for details). The extra states come from the added 7878, and are labeled by the index 00, i.e. D0,D¯0,T0,T¯0D_{0},\overline{D}_{0},T_{0},\overline{T}_{0}. We shall see that this extra row and column, together with a new vacuum compared to the model without 7878 now enable doublet-triplet splitting in the usual way (by fine-tuning). Note that all the doublets and triplets are located in a 55 or 4545 (or their conjugates) of SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5), except for one extra triplet in the 5050 of SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5).

The mass terms for the doublets and triplets are written as

(54)

and the off-diagonal blocks defined by

(59)

The separation of the matrix ℳ\mathcal{M} into 44 blocks is arbitrary and is used above merely as a simple way of presenting a large matrix. The matrix ℳdoublets\mathcal{M}_{\textrm{doublets}} is obtained out of ℳ\mathcal{M} by removing the last row and column, and taking α=−3\alpha=-3, β=−3\beta=-\sqrt{3}, while the matrix ℳtriplets\mathcal{M}_{\textrm{triplets}} is obtained by taking α=β=2\alpha=\beta=2. Note that the matrices were already simplified by taking the vacuum ansatz of vanishing VEVs

c1=d1=e2=f2=e5=f5=u1=u2=y\displaystyle c_{1}=d_{1}=e_{2}=f_{2}=e_{5}=f_{5}=u_{1}=u_{2}=y =0,\displaystyle=0, (60)

while the rest of the vacuum solution was not plugged-in. Notice also that the coefficients α\alpha and β\beta are located as factors in front of e4e_{4} or f4f_{4}; this is expected, since e4e_{4} and f4f_{4} are the SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5)-breaking VEVs, so they control the difference between the doublets and triplets. Also, the coefficients α\alpha are −3-3 and 22 for the doublets, respectively, which come from the VEV ⟨24⟩\langle 24\rangle in the terms 5⋅⟨24⟩⋅5¯5\cdot\langle 24\rangle\cdot\bar{5} of SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5). The coefficients β\beta are −3-\sqrt{3} and 22 for the doublets and triplets respectively, which are the Clebsch-Gordan coefficients coming from the terms 5⋅⟨24⟩⋅45¯5\cdot\langle 24\rangle\cdot\overline{45} or 5¯⋅⟨24⟩⋅45\bar{5}\cdot\langle 24\rangle\cdot 45 of SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5). One can check that this is indeed the case by locating the position of α\alpha and β\beta coefficients in ℳ\mathcal{M} and checking, to which states in Table 10 these matrix entries correspond to.

The procedure for fine-tuning is now similar to the one attempted in the 351′+351′¯+27+27¯351^{\prime}+\overline{351^{\prime}}+27+\overline{27} case in [11]. Once the vacuum solution is plugged-in, the determinants of the two matrices become zero:

det(ℳdoublets)|vacuum\displaystyle\det(\mathcal{M}_{\textrm{doublets}})\Big|_{\textrm{vacuum}} =0,\displaystyle=0, (61)
det(ℳtriplets)|vacuum\displaystyle\det(\mathcal{M}_{\textrm{triplets}})\Big|_{\textrm{vacuum}} =0.\displaystyle=0. (62)

The massless doublet-antidoublet and triplet-antitriplet pairs are simply the unphysical would-be Goldstone bosons from the breaking of E6\mathrm{E}_{6}. They correspond to the broken generators with the same quantum numbers, which can be found in SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10) language in the 1616 and 16¯\overline{16} parts of the adjoint 7878. The doublet-triplet splitting condition then requires another doublet-antidoublet pair to be massless, which imposes the following condition:

Cond⁡(ℳ)\displaystyle\mathrm{Cond}(\mathcal{M}) :=pmin1​ℳ,\displaystyle:=\mathrm{pmin}_{1}\mathcal{M}, (63)

where pmini\mathrm{pmin}_{i} denotes the ii-th principal minor of rank 11 (the subdeterminant when the ii-th row and column are removed). In our specific case, we chose to remove the first row and column, which correspond to the fields D0D_{0} and D¯0\overline{D}_{0}. We chose these due to simplicity, but note that this choice is valid only if the Goldstone modes of the given vacuum have nonzero D0D_{0} and D¯0\overline{D}_{0} components. This can be checked later on via equations (71) and (72). The logic behind the whole method is explained in Appendix C.

Given the notation above, DT-splitting can be performed by a fine-tuning, so that

Cond⁡(ℳdoublets)\displaystyle\mathrm{Cond}(\mathcal{M}_{\textrm{doublets}}) =0,\displaystyle=0, (64)
Cond⁡(ℳtriplets)\displaystyle\mathrm{Cond}(\mathcal{M}_{\textrm{triplets}}) ≠0.\displaystyle\neq 0. (65)

The above conditions can in principle be computed analytically, but they are too complicated to be of any practical use. The viability of the splitting conditions can be shown numerically though, as well as with some careful considerations. The most convenient way to perform the DT splitting is to make use of the dimensionless parameters λ5\lambda_{5} and λ6\lambda_{6} from the superpotential (see (5)). Since the invariants 27327^{3} and 27¯3\overline{27}^{3} have no all-singlet terms, λ5\lambda_{5} and λ6\lambda_{6} are not involved in the computation of the vacuum. Moreover, the matrix ℳ\mathcal{M} contains only a single entry with the parameter λ5\lambda_{5} and a single entry with the parameter λ6\lambda_{6}. The condition in equations (64) and (65) can be written as

K1−K2​λ5​λ6\displaystyle K_{1}-K_{2}\;\lambda_{5}\,\lambda_{6} =0,\displaystyle=0, (66)
K1′−K2′​λ5​λ6\displaystyle K^{\prime}_{1}-K^{\prime}_{2}\;\lambda_{5}\,\lambda_{6} ≠0,\displaystyle\neq 0, (67)

where K1,K2,K1′,K2′K_{1},K_{2},K^{\prime}_{1},K^{\prime}_{2} depend only on the other parameters in the Lagrangian (m351′m_{351^{\prime}}, m78m_{78}, m27m_{27}, λ1\lambda_{1}, λ2\lambda_{2}, λ3\lambda_{3}, λ4\lambda_{4}, λ7\lambda_{7}, λ8\lambda_{8}) and the vacuum itself, all of which can be computed independently from the parameters λ5\lambda_{5} and λ6\lambda_{6}. The analytic forms of KKs are not very illuminating, but they can easily be evaluated numerically for any values of the parameters m351′,m78,m27,λ1,λ2,λ3,λ4,λ7,λ8m_{351^{\prime}},m_{78},m_{27},\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3},\lambda_{4},\lambda_{7},\lambda_{8}. One can then take

λ5\displaystyle\lambda_{5} =K1K2​λ6,\displaystyle=\frac{K_{1}}{K_{2}\,\lambda_{6}}, (68)

with λ6\lambda_{6} arbitrary, and get an extra massless doublet mode. Substituting into condition (67), we can numerically check that indeed

K1′​K2\displaystyle K^{\prime}_{1}K_{2} ≠K2′​K1.\displaystyle\neq K^{\prime}_{2}K_{1}. (69)

We therefore conclude that the addition of the 7878 in the Higgs sector, both with the new vacuum and enlarged matrices ℳdoublets\mathcal{M}_{\textrm{doublets}} and ℳtriplets\mathcal{M}_{\textrm{triplets}}, now allows for a DT splitting in the model. Without the 7878, a similar attempt at fine-tuning is not possible, since in that case we get K2=K2′=0K_{2}=K^{\prime}_{2}=0 after inserting the vacuum and fine-tuning in λ5\lambda_{5} or λ6\lambda_{6} is not possible. Note that this tree-level fine-tuning is stable under quantum corrections due to the non-renormalization theorem for the superpotential.

The linear combinations of DDs and D¯\bar{D}s, which correspond to the MSSM Higgses HuH_{u} and HdH_{d}, can be found by computing the new left- and right- null-eigenvectors of the fine-tuned matrix ℳdoublets\mathcal{M}_{\textrm{doublets}}. In practice, the physical MSSM Higgses can most easily be extracted by computing the (left and right) null-eigenspace of the fine-tuned matrix ℳdoublets\mathcal{M}_{\textrm{doublets}}, which is 22-dimensional. Given any basis of the null-eigenspace, the Higgs will always be orthogonal to the would-be Goldstone boson. The would-be Goldstone itself can be easily identified by the fact that it has no component in the directions DiD_{i} (or D¯i\overline{D}_{i}) for i=1,3,4,5,7,8i=1,3,4,5,7,8. This absence of some doublets in the Goldstone can be deduced from the mass matrix in equation (55), but we also confirmed this by noting that the Goldstone components ϕi\phi_{i} are the ones which have couplings of their derivatives to the the gauge field through the following type of expression (originating from the kinetic terms of scalar fields):

−i​g​Aμa​(∂μϕi†)​(t^a​⟨ϕ⟩)i.\displaystyle-ig\,A_{\mu}^{a}\;(\partial^{\mu}\phi^{\dagger}_{i})\;(\hat{t}^{a}\langle\phi\rangle)^{i}. (70)

Choosing aa to be the doublet/antidoublet broken generators and using our vacuum, we identify the doublet components in ϕi†\phi^{\dagger}_{i} to which there is no coupling as indeed those listed above. Explicit computation identifies that the prevailing cause of some components not being present in the would-be Goldstone mode is our ansatz of vanishing VEVs. More precisely, without the vacuum ansatz, the terms in expression (70) can be schematically written as

We see that the absence of components DiD_{i} and D¯i\overline{D}_{i} for i=3,4,5,7,8i=3,4,5,7,8 are directly related to the vacuum ansatz with vanishing VEVs. D1D_{1} and D¯1\overline{D}_{1}, however, are always absent.77 7 The 2727 contains 22 singlets, but 33 doublets, so the singlets cannot be pushed to all the doublets with a tat^{a} generator, and thus one doublet component is missing. The representation 351′351^{\prime} has 55 singlets and 88 doublets, but the projection relation di​j​k​ 351′j​k=0d_{ijk}\,351^{\prime jk}=0 reshuffles the definitions of singlets and doublets, so there is no loss of doublet components.

The ratios of the various components of the Higgs, and hence the ratios of the EW VEVs of these component, are computed from the null-eigenspaces, while the magnitudes of the VEVs are given by the VEVs vu=⟨Hu⟩v_{u}=\langle H_{u}\rangle and vd=⟨Hd⟩v_{d}=\langle H_{d}\rangle. We have

vu2\displaystyle v_{u}^{2} =∑i=011|vi|2,\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{11}|{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}v_{i}}|^{2}, (73)
vd2\displaystyle v_{d}^{2} =∑i=011|v¯i|2,\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{11}|{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}\bar{v}_{i}}|^{2}, (74)

where vi=⟨Di⟩v_{i}=\langle D_{i}\rangle and v¯i=⟨D¯i⟩\bar{v}_{i}=\langle\overline{D}_{i}\rangle, and additionally the following MSSM relations hold:

vu2+vd2\displaystyle v_{u}^{2}+v_{d}^{2} =(246​GeV)2,\displaystyle=(246\,\mathrm{GeV})^{2}, (75)
vu/vd\displaystyle v_{u}/v_{d} =tan⁡β.\displaystyle=\tan\beta. (76)

5 Yukawa sector

The Yukawa sector comes from the Yukawa part of the superpotential after inserting the vacuum solution:

WYukawa\displaystyle W_{\textrm{Yukawa}} =27Fi​ 27Fj​(Y27i​j​⟨27⟩+Y351′¯i​j​⟨351′¯⟩).\displaystyle=27_{F}^{i}\;27_{F}^{j}\;\big(Y^{ij}_{27}\;\langle 27\rangle+Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\;\langle\overline{351^{\prime}}\rangle\,\big). (77)

In addition to the GUT scale VEVs in the representations 351′¯\overline{351^{\prime}} and 2727, the EW Higgses HuH_{u} and HdH_{d} also need to be present in both of these representations. The low-energy MSSM Higgses HuH_{u} and HdH_{d} come from a linear combination of the doublets of type D∼(1,2,+1/2)D\sim(1,2,+1/2) and antidoublets of the type D¯∼(1,2,−1/2)\overline{D}\sim(1,2,-1/2), respectively. These states are identified in Table 10, and their EW VEVs are labeled by vi:=⟨Di⟩v_{i}:=\langle D_{i}\rangle and v¯i:=⟨D¯i⟩\bar{v}_{i}:=\langle\overline{D}_{i}\rangle, where i=0,1,…,11i=0,1,\ldots,11. As discussed in section 4, we generically expect vi≠0v_{i}\neq 0 and v¯i≠0\bar{v}_{i}\neq 0.

Each generation of fermions is found in a fundamental representation 2727 of E6\mathrm{E}_{6}. The matter content of each generation, subdivided into SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10) representations, is the following:

The lepton doublet contains the electron ee and the neutrino ν\nu. and the right-handed neutrino νc\nu^{c}.

These exotic are labeled d′d^{\prime}, d′cd^{\prime c}, L′L^{\prime} and L′cL^{\prime c}, respectively.

As usual with vector-like states, the expressions for the low energy masses in equations (81)–(84) are nonlinear, which complicates the analysis of the masses. We comment more on the low-energy part of the Yukawa sector in section 6, in which we also do a numeric fit in the 2-generation case.

6 Numeric fit of the Yukawa sector

The presented model has 33 masses and 88 dimensionless parameters λi\lambda_{i} in the breaking sector, as well as two symmetric 3×33\times 3 Yukawa matrices in the Yukawa sector, which is easily seen from the superpotential in equation (1). Note also that the product λ5​λ6\lambda_{5}\lambda_{6} is fixed by the fine-tuning of the EW Higgs mass. Also, a rotation in family-space can bring one of the Yukawa matrices to be diagonal. We shall limit ourselves to the case where all parameters of the Lagrangian are real. The independent number of real parameters in the breaking sector is thus 3+8−1=103+8-1=10, while the 33-family Yukawa sector has 6+3=96+3=9 real parameters. Since the number of independent real parameters is 1919, while there are only 1717 real numbers to be measured (33 masses in the up, down, charged lepton sector each, the two differences of masses-squared in the neutrino sector, as well as 33 angles in each of the CKM and PMNS matrices; we neglect the CP-phases), the general expectation is that a fit is possible to perform. There may exist, however, non-obvious mass relations concealed due to the complexity of the low energy expressions in equations (81)–(84), which are not respected by the experimental values; these fears can be alleviated by finding points in parameter space, which give a good fit for to the masses and mixing angles.

In this section, we perform a fit in the simplified case of 22 families. Here, there are again 1010 real parameters in the breaking sector, while the Yukawa sector has 3+2=53+2=5 real parameters. The fit is performed for the results of the quark masses mtm_{t}, mcm_{c}, mbm_{b}, msm_{s}, the charged lepton masses mτm_{\tau} and mμm_{\mu}, the difference of the squared neutrino masses mν32−mν22m_{\nu_{3}}^{2}-m_{\nu_{2}}^{2}, and the mixing angles θc​b\theta_{cb} and θ23\theta_{23} in the CKM and PMNS matrices, respectively.

The most convenient way to perform the fit is to take some of the GUT scale VEVs as the parameters in the fit, instead of the initial parameters in the Lagrangian. This is advantageous since the equations of motion are linear in the Lagrangian parameters. Taking the ansatz c1=d1=e2=f2=e5=f5=u1=u2=y=0c_{1}=d_{1}=e_{2}=f_{2}=e_{5}=f_{5}=u_{1}=u_{2}=y=0, we need 1212 parameters; only 1010 are independent, while 22 are determined through the DD-terms. It is convenient, for example, to take the following quantities as independent parameters:

m351′,c2,d2,f1,f3,f4,e4,v,w,λ5.\displaystyle m_{351^{\prime}},\quad c_{2},\quad d_{2},\quad f_{1},\quad f_{3},\quad f_{4},\quad e_{4},\quad v,\quad w,\quad\lambda_{5}. (87)

We can then use the equations of motion to determine the remaining initial parameters and VEVs. The DD-terms are solved by taking

e3\displaystyle e_{3} =±|e4|2−|f4|2+2​|f3|2/2.\displaystyle=\pm\sqrt{|{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}e_{4}}|^{2}-|{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}f_{4}}|^{2}+2|{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}f_{3}}|^{2}}/\sqrt{2}. (89)

(101)

Using these values, λ6\lambda_{6} can then be determined by fine-tuning in the doublet mass matrix (see section 4), from which also the EW VEVs viv_{i} and v¯i\bar{v}_{i} are computed. One can then use these to compute the mass matrices from equations (81)–(84), and ultimately the masses and the mixing angles. For our numeric fit, we assume:

  • •

    the simplified case of second and third generation only;

  • •

    all parameters real;

  • •

    all errors in measured quantities at the 10%10\% level; we believe that at the present stage such a choice is a good compromise between the realistic case and the simplicity of the analysis;

  • •

    the values for the masses and mixing angles at the GUT scale ∼1016​GeV\sim 10^{16}\,\mathrm{GeV} as shown in Table 7 [26], valid for tan⁡β=10\tan{\beta}=10;

  • •

    positive signs in eqs. (88)-(89).

We performed the fit by minimizing the chi-squared function

χ2\displaystyle\chi^{2} :=∑i(fi​(x)−yi)σi2,\displaystyle:=\sum_{i}{\frac{(f_{i}(x)-y_{i})}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}}, (102)

with respect to the initial parameters xx. The experimental values are denoted by yiy_{i}, the values computed using our model are fi​(x)f_{i}(x), and σi\sigma_{i} are the 11-sigma deviations from the values yiy_{i}. For our fit, we have 99 different measured quantities, thus i=1,…,9i=1,\ldots,9. The errors are taken to be σi=0.1​yi\sigma_{i}=0.1\,y_{i}, giving

χ2=100​∑i(fi​(x)−yiyi)2.\displaystyle\chi^{2}=100\sum_{i}\left(\frac{f_{i}(x)-y_{i}}{y_{i}}\right)^{2}. (103)

We define the convenient measure χ^2=χ2/9\hat{\chi}^{2}=\chi^{2}/9, which tells us the average σ2\sigma^{2} deviation per measured value. Also, we define the pulls χi=(fi​(x)−yi)/σi\chi_{i}=(f_{i}(x)-y_{i})/\sigma_{i}, which tell us how many sigma a certain quantity deviates from the measured one.

Due to the large number of parameters, the χ2\chi^{2} function will have many local minima in the parameter space. We give below two such points in the parameter space, corresponding to the best fits that were found and which we deem sufficiently good (with χ^2≲1\hat{\chi}^{2}\lesssim 1). The results are given in Tables 3, 5, 7; the points in the parameter space are given in terms of the independent parameters best suited to a numeric search (as discussed in this section) in Table 3 and in terms of the original Lagrangian parameters in Table 5, while Table 7 shows the obtained results for the masses and mixing angles.

Notice from Tables 3 and 5 that of the two Yukawa matrices Y27Y_{27} and Y351′¯Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}, Y351′¯Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}} was chosen to be the diagonal one. Furthermore, the original Lagrangian parameters in Table 5 are given so that it can be checked they roughly fall into the perturbative regime. A possible exception could be the value λ8\lambda_{8} of the first solution.

Note that the given two points are merely the best ones we found. Due to the high dimensionality of the parameter space, we suspect there are likely many more points which give a comparable or a better fit. There are a number of observations that can be made about these points in general, however, by deducing them from the formulae, comparing the two parameter points given in the tables and through experience obtained by performing the fit:

  • •

    The parameter points are not necessarily close to each other, which also holds true for any specific single parameter. We can see in Table 3 that it is not necessary for any parameter to be at a very specific value to obtain a good fit. The suitable areas of parameter space thus form many disconnected regions, and no specific value can be claimed for any parameter. In this sense, the mass formulae of the theory are not very predictive of the original parameters.

  • •

    There is no specific mass or mixing angle, where one would consistently be getting tension. As observed from Table 7, while a specific solution might have most tension with observation coming from a single mass or mixing angle, there are other points, which also give a good fit and where this parameter is predicted better. In this sense we cannot claim any tendencies in tensions of the observables.

  • •

    Imagine that in Table 3 or 5 we rescale all the mass parameters with a common factor. Such a rescaling would have no influence on the masses of the quarks and charged leptons, which are controlled only by the EW VEVs, as can be seen from equations (81)–(83) and equation (85). Rescaling would influence the neutrino masses, however, due to the seesaw mechanism, confirmed by equation (84). In principle, the rescaling factor can always be adjusted, so that the fit of the mass-square difference of the neutrino masses mν32−mν22m_{\nu_{3}}^{2}-m_{\nu_{2}}^{2} is exact (provided this does not spoil the GUT scale, or the upper bounds on neutrino masses). Thus only neutrinos are actually sensitive to the GUT scale.

  • •

    The mass parameters are chosen to be at approximately the GUT scale, say at the order of 1015−16​GeV10^{15-16}\,\mathrm{GeV}. If this is true for all the mass parameters, there might be a problem with the neutrino masses. It is a well known fact that this GUT scale is a few orders of magnitude too large compared to the seesaw scale for sufficiently large mass differences in the neutrino sector. One can cure this problem by having the spontaneous symmetry breaking occur in multiple stages, with a mass hierarchy between different VEVs and the seesaw scale corresponding to one of the intermediate stages. The gauge coupling unification in such a scenario could then be spoilt by the particles appearing at these intermediate mass scales.

    In our case, however, the number of different VEVs is large enough, so that having one or two of the VEVs at a smaller scale does not disturb the breaking pattern. To see this, note that to obtain sufficiently large neutrino masses, it is enough for one of the terms in equation (84) to be of the proper scale, which can be achieved by simply taking f1f_{1} or f3f_{3} to be several orders of magnitude smaller than the GUT scale (the seesaw type I contributions). In the solutions given in Table 3, we achieved sufficiently high neutrino masses by taking the parameterf1f_{1} (and also vv) to be a few orders of magnitude below the GUT scale. As seen from the gauge boson masses in Table (8), small f1f_{1} and vv do not spoil the one-stage breaking scenario; since the intermediate scales are not associated to an intermediate symmetry breaking at that scale, but are instead purely accidental due to a carefully chosen parameter point, we do not expect too many relevant states (apart from the singlets νc\nu^{c} with f1f_{1} Majorana mass) to be found at the scale f1f_{1}. We noticed however the appearance of a lighter color triplet-antitriplet pair, possibly due to the similarities between the doublet and triplet mass matrices. Although this influences the running of the gauge couplings, we will neglect it in view of the (presumably) large threshold uncertainties present anyway.

  • •

    A final comment on the neutrino masses: although only the difference of masses-squared needs to be fitted, one still needs to check that the neutrino masses themselves are <1​eV<1\,\mathrm{eV} [27]. As seen in Table 7, this condition holds true for both of our parameter points.

7 Discussion

What we presented here is a model we believe is a good candidate for a minimal supersymmetric renormalizable E6E_{6} GUT. Let’s see why this model can be considered as more minimal than our previous candidate [11]. Although the total number of degrees of freedom is now larger (78>27+2778>27+27), what really counts are the number of multiplets and, even more important, the total number of free parameters. The number of parameters in the Higgs sector is now 11 complex minus 5 phases due to field redefinitions. Yukawa sector adds another 3 real and 6 complex parameters. Together with one real gauge coupling we have thus a total of 3333 real parameters. This is 7 more than in the minimal SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10) [13, 14, 15], but still 1616 less than even in the simplified truncated version of E6E_{6} in [11].

Is there any possible low-energy signature of this model? It is often said that E6E_{6} could have possible light extra generations, coming from remnants of the three copies of the 27F27_{F}. Light vector-like fermions of the SM group could indeed emerge out of E6\mathrm{E}_{6} if they were associated with anomaly cancellation in a TeV\mathrm{TeV}-scale extra U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1). In such a setup, the extra U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1) would be a linear combination of the two U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1)s present in the rank 66 group E6\mathrm{E}_{6}. Phenomenology of such TeV\mathrm{TeV} scale E6\mathrm{E}_{6} motivated models has been extensively studied, see for eg. [28]. In the present setup, however, there are no intermediate U⁡(1)\mathrm{U}(1)s and any light vector-like states would be accidental. In fact if we try to get such light states from our solution, we find them hard to obtain. The question is, does the matrix for (as an example) down quarks in eq. (78) allow 4 or more zero eigenvalues once we limit all v¯\bar{v}’s to zero? This can in principle be obtained either by putting c2,f4→0c_{2},f_{4}\to 0 (remember that our solution already has c1=f5=0c_{1}=f_{5}=0), or by imposing a vanishing determinant constraint to Yukawa matrices. The first case points towards an SU(5) invariant vacuum1010 10 This can be easily seen from the expression for λ2\lambda_{2} in (97): if f4→0f_{4}\to 0, we need either e3→0e_{3}\to 0 or e4→0e_{4}\to 0; both lead to an SU(5) invariant vacuum with e4,f4→0e_{4},f_{4}\to 0, see (89)., while the second one constrains the Yukawa parameters and so a worse fit to data is expected. So we conclude that such an extreme, albeit interesting situation is unlikely, at least in the given vacuum solution. Although we cannot make the same conclusions in general, any possibility of light states, if available, will occur due to fine-tuning in the superpotential parameters.

Another possibility for having light states could be to have flat directions. We checked by explicit computation that no such states are present in our solution. Although we omit the details of this computation here, the interested reader can reconstruct the mass matrix of the SM singlets via the all-singlet terms in the superpotential, which are given in equations (6)–(16). If the vacuum solution is then plugged-in, one discovers 44 massless singlet states, all of which are in fact would-be Goldstone bosons. Note that the adjoint 7878 of E6\mathrm{E}_{6} contains 55 SM singlets, while only 11 remains unbroken among the SM generators, so the 44 massless singlet states are the would-be Goldstone bosons eaten up by the 44 broken singlet generators. We thus conclude there are no physical massless singlet states. Other vacua could in principle be possible: one of them is described in Appendix D.

Proton decay is, as usual, quite hidden by details of superpartners’ spectra: it is hard to disentangle the GUT and SUSY breaking information from it. Once however colliders will (hopefully) tell us more about the low energy spectrum, this E6E_{6} theory as well as other grand unified theories could be tested better. For the sake of completeness the forms of the low-energy D=5D=5 operators are given in Appendix E.

The model we presented here is the minimal known E6E_{6}, although for a more convincing proof we should satisfy three more checks.

  • •

    First, there is a possibility to redefine the charges under matter parity, so that the 27+27¯27+\overline{27} parity is now transferred to the fermionic sector. This means that the fields 351′+351′¯+78351^{\prime}+\overline{351^{\prime}}+78 should alone break to the SM gauge group as well as allow for DT splitting. The fermionic sector would now consists of 27Fa27^{a}_{F}, a=1,…,4a=1,\ldots,4 and 27¯F\overline{27}_{F}. The Yukawa terms could be written schematically as

    (27Fa27¯F)T​(Y351′¯a​b​⟨351′¯⟩m27a+λa​⟨78⟩m27b+λb​⟨78⟩y351′​⟨351′⟩)​(27Fb27¯F).\displaystyle\begin{pmatrix}27^{a}_{F}\\ \overline{27}_{F}\end{pmatrix}^{T}\begin{pmatrix}Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ab}\langle\overline{351^{\prime}}\rangle&m_{27}^{a}+\lambda^{a}\langle 78\rangle\\ m_{27}^{b}+\lambda^{b}\langle 78\rangle&y_{351^{\prime}}\langle 351^{\prime}\rangle\\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}27^{b}_{F}\\ \overline{27}_{F}\end{pmatrix}. (104)

    The total number of parameters is now the following: 5 complex parameters come from the Higgs superpotential, 3 phases of which can be rotated away by Higgs field redefinitions; 4 real diagonal components are given by the only Yukawa matrix, and 8 complex and one real parameters are the off-diagonal terms; finally, 1 real gauge coupling sums to a total of 29 real free parameters. This would be 4 real parameters less than the model in this paper. Obviously there is no guarantee that such a model is realistic. We plan to come back to this issue in the future.

  • •

    Second, we should study the complete three generation case, not only its two generation subsystem. Although the number of parameters seems naively large enough, it is far from obvious that a successful fit is possible. In fact already in the two generation case considered here we could not find a solution with vanishing χ2\chi^{2}, in spite of enough free parameters. However the (at least partially) successful fit of the the minimal SO(10) analogous case [29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 19, 20, 37, 38, 39] with 1010 and 126¯\overline{126} (instead of 2727 and 351′¯\overline{351^{\prime}}) Yukawa couplings make us feel optimistic. Notice also that the usual obstruction of the neutrino mass either too low or unification violated [16, 17, 18, 19] is here avoided as shown in section 6.

  • •

    Third, the theory is not asymptotically free and has a huge gauge coupling beta function, more precisely 159159. This means, similarly as in our previous E6E_{6} model, or the minimal renormalizable supersymmetric SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10), that a Landau pole is close to the GUT scale and so the theory itself may be already in the non-perturbative regime. An indication of problems being present already at the matching scale MG​U​TM_{GUT} can be found in the calculation of the threshold corrections [40, 41]. The general problem of having large numbers of degrees of freedom (in our case through large representations) and the associated non-perturbativity is a problem, which is far from easy to solve and well beyond the purpose of this paper, although some progress has been made recently [42, 43] based on previous works on Seiberg dualities. We hope to come back to this very interesting issue soon.

But even in the case the model presented here is the minimal one, other vacua could still be realistic with in principle different predictions.

Appendix A Gauge Boson masses

We compute in this appendix the expression for the gauge boson masses, so that we can confirm that solutions really break into the SM group. We write the mass terms in the Lagrangian as

ℒm​a​s​s\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{mass} =g2​Aμa​Ma​b​Aμ​b,\displaystyle=g^{2}A_{\mu}^{\;a}M^{ab}A^{\mu\,b}, (105)

where gg is the E6\mathrm{E}_{6} coupling constant and the matrix Ma​bM^{ab} is computed via

Ma​b\displaystyle M^{ab} :=∑iTr⁡((t^a​⟨ϕi⟩)†​(t^b​⟨ϕi⟩)).\displaystyle:=\sum_{i}\mathrm{Tr}\left(\left(\hat{t}^{a}\langle\phi_{i}\rangle\right)^{\dagger}\left(\hat{t}^{b}\langle\phi_{i}\rangle\right)\right). (106)

The sum is over all representations containing VEVs (contributions come from the representations of the breaking sector), while t^a\hat{t}^{a} denotes the action of the aa-th generator on the representation ϕi\phi_{i}. The mass matrix becomes block diagonal if we choose an appropriate basis (indices a,ba,b), so that the basis gauge bosons have well defined transformation properties under the SM group (note that some of these states are complex). We omit the details of this calculation and only give the results, collected in Table 8.

Appendix B Particle identification

In this appendix, we write the definitions of various states needed in the paper. The SM singlet VEVs were already defined in Table 1. We supplement the list of definitions with Tables 10 and 11. In Table 10 we define the doublets (1,2,+1/2)(1,2,+1/2), antidoublets (1,2,−1/2)(1,2,-1/2), triplets (3,1,−1/3)(3,1,-1/3) and antitriplets (3¯,1,+1/3)(\bar{3},1,+1/3); these definitions are needed for DT splitting. In Table 11, we define the weak triplets (1,3,±1)(1,3,\pm 1) relevant for type II seesaw. All the states in the two-index 351′351^{\prime} can be specified by writing the basis states of this representation by using two labels of the fundamental 2727. In this notation, both labels are SM representation in the 2727, assumed to have all the color and weak indices contracted in the correct manner to obtain the desired SM state in the 351′351^{\prime}. More details on this notation can be found in [11].

Appendix C DT splitting and Goldstone modes

Analysis of the DT splitting in the group E6\mathrm{E}_{6} is complicated by the fact that a vacuum breaking to the SM group will automatically cause a doublet and a triplet mode to be massless. These massless modes are would-be Goldstone bosons: E6→SM\mathrm{E}_{6}\to\mathrm{SM} causes the breaking of 78−12=6678-12=66 generators, with a doublet-antidoublet and triplet-antitriplet pair among them. One possible procedure to compute the condition for an extra massless mode in a matrix MM, for which det​M=0\mathrm{det}\,M=0, is to take

limε→0(det(M−ε​I)/ε)⟨e|f⟩\displaystyle\frac{\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\big(\det(M-\varepsilon I)/\varepsilon\big)}{\langle e|f\rangle} =0,\displaystyle=0, (107)

where ee and ff are the already present left and right null-eigenvectors of MM, respectively. We present below, however, a simplified procedure of computing the conditions of DT splitting in the presence of a Goldstone mode. Its advantages are that it is computationally less intensive and that no issues with singularities, such as ⟨e|f⟩\langle e|f\rangle=0, arise in the procedure.

Suppose we use a generic label AA for an n×nn\times n complex matrix. Although the true scalar mass-squared matrix is in fact the hermitian and positive definite matrix A†​AA^{\dagger}A, it is more efficient to work with AA. AA might not necessarily be diagonalizable, but it has a singular value decomposition. The presence of a zero eigenmode in A†​AA^{\dagger}A implies

det​A\displaystyle\mathrm{det}\,A =0.\displaystyle=0. (108)

We will rotate this matrix into a basis, where the left and right Goldstone modes correspond to the first basis vector of the rows and columns, respectively. We first write AA in (1+(n−1))×(1+(n−1))(1+(n-1))\times(1+(n-1)) block form:

A\displaystyle A =(m𝐦𝐑†𝐦𝐋𝐌),\displaystyle=\begin{pmatrix}m&\mathbf{m_{R}}^{\dagger}\\ \mathbf{m_{L}}&\mathbf{M}\\ \end{pmatrix}, (109)

where boldface small letters denote n−1n-1 column vectors, and boldface capital letters denote matrices. Since AA has a massless mode, there exist left and right null-eigenvectors e→0\vec{e}_{0} and f→0\vec{f}_{0}, respectively:

A†​e→0\displaystyle A^{\dagger}\vec{e}_{0} =0,\displaystyle=0, A​f→0\displaystyle A\vec{f}_{0} =0.\displaystyle=0. (110)

Providing we choose the phases such that the first components of e→0\vec{e}_{0} and f→0\vec{f}_{0} are positive, we define (n−1)(n-1) column vectors 𝐞\mathbf{e} and 𝐟\mathbf{f} via

e→0|e→0|\displaystyle\frac{\vec{e}_{0}}{|\vec{e}_{0}|} =:(1−𝐞†​𝐞𝐞)\displaystyle=:\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{1-\mathbf{e}^{\dagger}\mathbf{e}}\\ \mathbf{e}\\ \end{pmatrix} f→0|f→0|\displaystyle\frac{\vec{f}_{0}}{|\vec{f}_{0}|} =:(1−𝐟†​𝐟𝐟).\displaystyle=:\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{1-\mathbf{f}^{\dagger}\mathbf{f}}\\ \mathbf{f}\\ \end{pmatrix}. (111)

Writing the null-eigenvector conditions in equations (110) in block form, we get 33 independent equations (two (n−1)(n-1)-vector, 11 scalar):

1−𝐞†​𝐞​𝐦𝐑+𝐌†​𝐞\displaystyle\sqrt{1-\mathbf{e}^{\dagger}\mathbf{e}}\;\mathbf{m_{R}}+\mathbf{M}^{\dagger}\,\mathbf{e} =0,\displaystyle=0, (112)
1−𝐟†​𝐟​𝐦𝐋+𝐌​𝐟\displaystyle\sqrt{1-\mathbf{f}^{\dagger}\mathbf{f}}\;\mathbf{m_{L}}+\mathbf{M}^{\phantom{\dagger}}\,\mathbf{f} =0,\displaystyle=0, (113)
m​1−𝐞†​𝐞​1−𝐟†​𝐟−𝐞†​𝐌​𝐟\displaystyle m\sqrt{1-\mathbf{e}^{\dagger}\mathbf{e}}\sqrt{1-\mathbf{f}^{\dagger}\mathbf{f}}-\mathbf{e}^{\dagger}\,\mathbf{M}\,\mathbf{f} =0\displaystyle=0 (114)

These can for example be used to define mm, 𝐦𝐋\mathbf{m_{L}} and 𝐦𝐑\mathbf{m_{R}} in terms of 𝐌\mathbf{M}, 𝐞\mathbf{e} and 𝐟\mathbf{f}. We now define a n×nn\times n unitary matrix U⁡(𝐱)U(\mathbf{x}), whose form will be useful for rotating the basis of AA: in block form, UU is written as

U⁡(𝐱):=(1−𝐱†​𝐱𝐱†−𝐱Λ⁡(𝐱)),\displaystyle U(\mathbf{x}):=\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{1-\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\mathbf{x}}&\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\\ -\mathbf{x}&\Lambda(\mathbf{x})\\ \end{pmatrix}, (115)

where

Λ⁡(𝐱):=I−𝐱​𝐱†1+1−𝐱†​𝐱.\displaystyle\Lambda(\mathbf{x}):=I-\frac{\mathbf{x}\,\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}}{1+\sqrt{1-\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\mathbf{x}}}. (116)

It is possible to check explicitly that UU is indeed unitary and that the following relations hold:

U⁡(𝐱)​U​(𝐱)†\displaystyle U(\mathbf{x})\,U(\mathbf{x})^{\dagger} =I,\displaystyle=I, (117)
U​(𝐱)−1=U​(𝐱)†\displaystyle U(\mathbf{x})^{-1}=U(\mathbf{x})^{\dagger} =U⁡(−𝐱),\displaystyle=U(-\mathbf{x}), (118)
Λ​(𝐱)†\displaystyle\Lambda(\mathbf{x})^{\dagger} =Λ⁡(𝐱)=Λ⁡(−𝐱),\displaystyle=\Lambda(\mathbf{x})=\Lambda(-\mathbf{x}), (119)
Λ​(𝐱)−1\displaystyle\Lambda(\mathbf{x})^{-1} =I+𝐱​𝐱†1−𝐱†​𝐱​(1+1−𝐱†​𝐱),\displaystyle=I+\frac{\mathbf{x}\,\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}}{\sqrt{1-\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\mathbf{x}}\;(1+\sqrt{1-\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\mathbf{x}})}, (120)
det​Λ​(𝐱)\displaystyle\mathrm{det}\Lambda(\mathbf{x}) =1−𝐱†​𝐱1+1−𝐱†​𝐱.\displaystyle=1-\frac{\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\mathbf{x}}{1+\sqrt{1-\mathbf{x}^{\dagger}\mathbf{x}}}. (121)

The properly rotated matrix AA, denoted by A′A^{\prime}, is then by explicit computation equal to

A′\displaystyle A^{\prime} :=U⁡(𝐞)​A​U​(𝐟)−1=(0𝟎†𝟎𝐌𝐫𝐨𝐭),\displaystyle:=U(\mathbf{e})\,A\,U(\mathbf{f})^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathbf{0}^{\dagger}\\ \mathbf{0}&\mathbf{M_{rot}}\\ \end{pmatrix}, (122)

where

𝐌𝐫𝐨𝐭\displaystyle\mathbf{M_{rot}} =Λ​(𝐞)−1​𝐌​Λ​(𝐟)−1.\displaystyle=\Lambda(\mathbf{e})^{-1}\mathbf{M}\,\Lambda(\mathbf{f})^{-1}. (123)

We have indeed rotated into a basis, where the first column and row correspond to the zero eigenmodes. Crucially, the formula for the rotated (n−1)×(n−1)(n-1)\times(n-1) block has only one term, where a simple biunitary rotation is performed on the original block 𝐌\mathbf{M}; another zero-eigenmode can now be simply imposed by taking det​𝐌𝐫𝐨𝐭=0\mathrm{det}\mathbf{M_{rot}}=0. But since we now have

det​𝐌\displaystyle\mathrm{det}\mathbf{M} =det​𝐌𝐫𝐨𝐭​det​(Λ⁡(𝐞)​Λ​(𝐟)).\displaystyle=\mathrm{det}\mathbf{M_{rot}}\;\mathrm{det}\big(\Lambda(\mathbf{e})\Lambda(\mathbf{f})\big). (124)

it is sufficient to impose det𝐌=0\det\mathbf{M}=0. The only possible caveat is the possibility that either det​Λ​(𝐞)=0\mathrm{det}\,\Lambda(\mathbf{e})=0 or det​Λ​(𝐟)=0\mathrm{det}\,\Lambda(\mathbf{f})=0; considering equation (121) and that 𝐞\mathbf{e} and 𝐟\mathbf{f} are parts of normalized vectors, this can happen only if 𝐞†​𝐞=1\mathbf{e}^{\dagger}\mathbf{e}=1 or 𝐟†​𝐟=1\mathbf{f}^{\dagger}\mathbf{f}=1, which would imply that the zero modes of AA have a zero component in the direction of the first vector of the original basis. But since the eigenvalues of A†​AA^{\dagger}A (the determinant of A†​A−λ​IA^{\dagger}A-\lambda I) do not change if we rearrange the rows or the columns of AA, we can always rearrange the original basis so that we take the ii-th row and the jj-th column to be the preferred one for the left and right null-eigenmodes, respectively.

The main result thus states the following: if an n×nn\times n complex matrix AA has a zero mode present, an additional zero mode is obtained by demanding the (i,j)(i,j)-th minor of AA to vanish (the subdeterminant of AA, when the ii-th row and jj-th column are removed), where the indices ii and jj can be arbitrarily chosen, as long as the left and right null-eigenvectors of AA have respectively a nonzero ii-th and jj-th component.

Appendix D An alternative vacuum

The Yukawa fit presented in this paper is based on the vacuum computed in section 3. Since we have not been able to obtain (yet) a full classification of all vacua in this E6\mathrm{E}_{6} model, we cannot conclude much about the broader possibilities of suitable vacua (especially the Yukawa sector), but we were able to find one other alternative Standard Model vacuum. We can obtain it by taking the following ansatz of vanishing VEVs:

c2=d2=e5=f5=e2=f2=u1=u2=y\displaystyle c_{2}=d_{2}=e_{5}=f_{5}=e_{2}=f_{2}=u_{1}=u_{2}=y =0.\displaystyle=0. (125)

This ansatz is similar to the ansatz of the original vacuum, but the vanishing of e5,f5e_{5},f_{5} is now paired up with the vanishing of c2,d2c_{2},d_{2} instead of c1,d1c_{1},d_{1}. For the purposes of this appendix, we omit the specific form of the solutions, as well as other details, such as the check that the unbroken group is indeed that of the Standard Model.

Looking at the Yukawa terms in equation (78), we see that the alternative vacuum with c2=f5=0c_{2}=f_{5}=0 decouples the 16F16_{F} from the 10F10_{F} of SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10) (in leading order of mE​W/MG​U​Tm_{EW}/M_{GUT}). The heavy vector-like exotics (in the down-quark sector and charged lepton sector) in the fermionic 27F27_{F} are thus purely in the 10F10_{F} part. The low-energy mass matrices are thus simply those for the 16F16_{F}, the analysis of the Yukawa sector becomes linear, and numerically one can make use of the fit for the minimal supersymmetric SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10) model [29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 19, 20, 37, 38, 39] with the Higgs in the 1010 and 126¯\overline{126} coupling to fermion pairs in 16F216_{F}^{2}.

The intriguing possibility of this alternative vacuum, which recovers the SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10) limit, is somewhat marred by issues in DT splitting. Given the ansatz in equation (125), the doublet and triplet mass matrices become block diagonal with the following block form (with the basis of the barred states rearranged in the same order as for unbarred):

[D0D3D6D9D10D11],[D1D2D4D5],[D7D8],\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}D_{0}&D_{3}&D_{6}&D_{9}&D_{10}&D_{11}\\ \end{bmatrix},\quad\begin{bmatrix}D_{1}&D_{2}&D_{4}&D_{5}\\ \end{bmatrix},\quad\begin{bmatrix}D_{7}&D_{8}\\ \end{bmatrix}, (126)
[T0T3T6T9T10T11],[T1T2T4T5],[T7T8T12].\displaystyle\begin{bmatrix}T_{0}&T_{3}&T_{6}&T_{9}&T_{10}&T_{11}\\ \end{bmatrix},\quad\begin{bmatrix}T_{1}&T_{2}&T_{4}&T_{5}\\ \end{bmatrix},\quad\begin{bmatrix}T_{7}&T_{8}&T_{12}\\ \end{bmatrix}. (127)

The Goldstone modes, for example, turn out to be in the first block. The problem now is, however, that a fine-tuning is block specific: the light Higgs lives only in one of the blocks. We see from equation (78) that the low-energy fermionic mass matrices MDTM_{D}^{T} and MEM_{E} are now controlled solely by the EW VEVs v¯2\bar{v}_{2}, v¯4\bar{v}_{4} and v¯8\bar{v}_{8}. In the v¯8=0\bar{v}_{8}=0 case, we get the unwanted mass relation MDT=MEM_{D}^{T}=M_{E}, but D¯8\overline{D}_{8} is in a separate block compared to D¯2\overline{D}_{2} and D¯4\overline{D}_{4}. A realistic pattern of fermion masses would thus require a double fine-tuning: one in the second block and one in the third block. Due to this feature, we consider this vacuum to be of less interest: beside the aesthetically unpleasing extra fine-tuning, the additional light Higgs pair Hu′+Hd′H^{\prime}_{u}+H^{\prime}_{d} pair gives large threshold corrections in the running of the gauge couplings, possibly spoiling unification. The model contains many heavy states though, so the situation regarding the RGE is not clear-cut. For determining the feasibility of this vacuum, further investigation would be necessary.

We conclude this section of the Appendix with a brief elaboration on which kind of ansatz is suitable for a good vacuum, i.e. we motivate equations (29)–(30) and (125). The considerations will be very similar to the ones in the E6\mathrm{E}_{6} breaking sector, where the 7878 is omitted [11] and a full classification of vacua is known. Suppose we look for a specific vacuum solution: we want it to be as simple as possible (it has as many vanishing VEVs as possible), yet it needs to be able to break E6\mathrm{E}_{6} to the SM group. Due to the DD-terms in SUSY, we assume a conjugate-symmetric ansatz, where a vanishing VEV in 2727 or 351′351^{\prime} implies that the corresponding (conjugate) VEV in the 27¯\overline{27} or 351′¯\overline{351^{\prime}} also vanishes, and vice versa. First, we identify the SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5) breaking VEVs from Table 1: e4e_{4}, e5e_{5}, f4f_{4}, f5f_{5} and yy. The FyF_{y} equation of motion automatically implies y=0y=0. Since SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5) needs to be broken, either the pair e4e_{4}, f4f_{4} is non-vanishing, or the pair e5e_{5}, f5f_{5}. Considerations of alignment symmetry in [11] imply that the choice is irrelevant, since these pairs are exchanged if one changes the embedding of SO⁡(10)\mathrm{SO}(10) in E6\mathrm{E}_{6}, such that the two 5¯\bar{5}s of SU⁡(5)\mathrm{SU}(5) in the 2727 are exchanged. Therefore one pair needs to be necessarily non-zero, while we can try a vanishing ansatz for the other pair. In the 27+27¯27+\overline{27} part of the breaking sector, the pairs c1c_{1}, d1d_{1} and c2c_{2}, d2d_{2} also get exchanged under alignment symmetry; we assume one pair to be non-zero (such that the 27+27¯27+\overline{27} part does indeed contribute to the symmetry breaking), but we can again try setting the other pair to vanish in the simple ansatz. The choice of the vanishing pair now points to either the scenario of the main vacuum of this paper, or the the alternative vacuum presented in this appendix. The remaining part of the ansatz, e2=f2=0e_{2}=f_{2}=0 (which transforms into itself under alignment symmetry), is suggested from the solutions in the model without the 7878, while u1=u2=0u_{1}=u_{2}=0 then follows as a consequence of the FF-terms. We finish the ansatz discussion with the following points:

  • •

    The main vacuum solution of the paper follows from the ansatz, which is a direct extension of the solution ansatz in the absence of the 7878 [11]. There, the EOMs were simpler, and this ansatz actually represented the most general SM solution once gauge freedom and the FF-term equations were accounted for. Note that only the ansatz can be extended, the main solution itself is not merely an extension of the solution when the 7878 is omitted.

  • •

    The alternative ansatz leads to a SM vacuum only after the 7878 was included; there is no such option if the 7878 is omitted.

  • •

    A complete classification would tell us, whether still other nonequivalent vacua exist, where the VEVs are non-vanishing. If the 7878 is omitted, such vacua did not exist, but we expect this situation to change due to more terms and more VEVs in the EOM.

Appendix E Proton decay

For completeness let’s summarize the analysis of D=5D=5 proton decay in this model, similar to the analysis done in [11], obtaining analogous results. The low-energy operators in the superpotential, which are relevant for proton decay, are

W|proton\displaystyle W\big|_{\textrm{proton}} =−[(C¯1i​n​A−C¯1′i​m​A(XT)m)n[(1+X∗XT)−1/2]n(ℳ^T−1)A​BjC1k​l​B]QiL^jQkQl\displaystyle=-\Big[\big(\overline{C}_{1}^{inA}-\overline{C}_{1}^{\prime imA}(X^{T})_{m}{}^{n}\big)\big[(1+X^{\ast}X^{T})^{-1/2}\big]_{n}{}^{j}\;(\hat{\mathcal{M}}_{T}^{-1})_{AB}\;C_{1}^{klB}\Big]\;Q_{i}\hat{L}_{j}Q_{k}Q_{l}
−[(C¯2n​j​A+23C¯2′m​j​A(XT)m)n[(1+49X∗XT)−1/2]n(ℳ^T−1)A​BiC2k​l​B]d^icujcukcelc,\displaystyle\quad-\Big[\big(\overline{C}_{2}^{njA}+\tfrac{2}{3}\overline{C}_{2}^{\prime mjA}(X^{T})_{m}{}^{n}\big)\big[(1+\tfrac{4}{9}X^{\ast}X^{T})^{-1/2}\big]_{n}{}^{i}\;(\hat{\mathcal{M}}_{T}^{-1})_{AB}\;C_{2}^{klB}\Big]\;\hat{d}^{c}_{i}u^{c}_{j}u^{c}_{k}e^{c}_{l}, (128)

with the XX defined in equation (85) and the mass matrix of ℳT\mathcal{M}_{\textrm{T}} as already defined in equation (55) of section 4. Note that the ℳT\mathcal{M}_{\textrm{T}} has a zero eigenmode corresponding to the would-be Goldstone, so its inverse cannot be directly computed; we instead write ℳ^T−1=limM→∞(ℳT+M​e​fT)−1\hat{\mathcal{M}}_{T}^{-1}=\lim_{M\to\infty}(\mathcal{M}_{T}+M\;e\,f^{T})^{-1}, with ee and ff being the left and right column-eigenvectors of ℳT\mathcal{M}_{T}, respectively.

The CC coefficients are computed to be

2​C1i​j​A\displaystyle 2\;C_{1}^{ijA} =−Y27i​jδA1+12​10Y351′¯i​jδA5−12​6Y351′¯i​jδA7−12​3Y351′¯i​jδA12,\displaystyle=-Y_{27}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{1}+\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{5}-\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{7}-\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{3}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{12}, (129)
2​C2i​j​A\displaystyle 2\;C_{2}^{ijA} =−Y27i​jδA1+12​10Y351′¯i​jδA5−12​6Y351′¯i​jδA7+22​3Y351′¯i​jδA12,\displaystyle=-Y_{27}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{1}+\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{5}-\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{6}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{7}+\tfrac{2}{2\sqrt{3}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{12}, (130)
2​C¯1i​j​A\displaystyle 2\;\overline{C}_{1}^{ijA} =−Y27i​jδA2+12​10Y351′¯i​jδA4+12​2Y351′¯i​jδA8,\displaystyle=-Y_{27}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{2}+\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{4}+\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{8}, (131)
2​C¯1′i​j​A\displaystyle 2\,\overline{C}_{1}^{\prime ijA} =Y27i​jδA3−12​10Y351′¯i​jδA9−12​2Y351′¯i​jδA11,\displaystyle=\phantom{-}Y_{27}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{3}-\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{9}-\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{11}, (132)
2​C¯2i​j​A\displaystyle 2\;\overline{C}_{2}^{ijA} =−Y27i​jδA2+12​10Y351′¯i​jδA4−12​2Y351′¯i​jδA8,\displaystyle=-Y_{27}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{2}+\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{4}-\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{8}, (133)
2​C¯2′i​j​A\displaystyle 2\,\overline{C}_{2}^{\prime ijA} =Y27i​jδA3−12​10Y351′¯i​jδA9+12​2Y351′¯i​jδA11.\displaystyle=\phantom{-}Y_{27}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{3}-\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{10}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{9}+\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\,Y_{\overline{351^{\prime}}}^{ij}\,\delta^{A}{}_{11}. (134)

We see that the CC-coefficients are the same as the coefficients in [11], if we cross out the contributions from the extra Yukawa term in that model. More specifically, notice that there are no A=0A=0 contributions from triplets/antitriplets in the new representation 7878, since the 7878 is not present in the Yukawa sector (it does not couple to two 27F27_{F}’s).

Once the model parameters are fit to the experimental values of the fermion masses and mixings, the four-fermion amplitude mediating proton decay is fixed and thus potentially dangerous, but it can always be suppressed by implementing a split supersymmetric scenario without changing any other conclusion.
